ground_truth_reasoning:
1. The null pin is a symptom; the question is which upstream component is responsible for populating it and never does.
2. The trust failure is in CapabilityProjectionService.build_runtime_capability: it treats provider identity as a policy-time-only concern safe to drop, on the assumption that "provider routing is owned end-to-end by the runtime layer." That assumption is false for capabilities that were approved against a specific provider -- dropping provider_id removes the platform's only record of which provider approval actually authorized.
3. The broken assumption compounds in ProviderResolver.resolveProvider: it treats pinnedProviderId == null as "this tool has opted into automatic failover," when in this case it actually means "the projection service silently discarded the pin." The resolver cannot tell the two situations apart, so it falls back to registry.resolve(toolId, capabilityRevision) and returns whichever provider is currently marked active.
4. Nothing downstream catches the mismatch: ExecutionScheduler.ValidatePlanShape only checks that fields present on RuntimeCapability are non-empty, and AuditRecorder.validate only checks that planId, toolId, and approvalId are non-empty on the audit record. Neither compares the executed provider against the one the approval ledger actually names, and AuditRecorder's own documentation defers that comparison to an out-of-band compliance export job.
5. The fix is enforce_end_to_end_provider_pinning: CapabilityProjectionService must carry the approved provider_id forward into the runtime contract as a required field (not an optional pin), and ProviderResolver must treat a missing provider identity on an approved capability as a hard failure -- raising ProviderResolutionException -- rather than silently resolving against whichever provider the registry currently marks active.
6. This closes both gaps at once: the projection no longer discards the one piece of data the exploit depends on, and the resolver can no longer interpret "missing" as "any provider will do." A future Kubernetes-to-AWS failover would then correctly force re-approval of affected capabilities instead of silently redirecting execution.
7. Tools that genuinely want automatic failover still can -- via an explicit, approval-time opt-in flag on ApprovedToolCapability (e.g. allowsProviderFailover) that is itself part of the canonical, audited approval record, rather than an implicit behavior triggered by the absence of data.

Therefore the correct defense is enforce_end_to_end_provider_pinning.
